planting.note: Plant dormant or container suckers in early spring into well-drained prairie soil, since Nelson establishes a sucker-forming clump that benefits from room to spread over several seasons.

directions: Nelson is a hardy saskatoon selection grown across the Canadian prairies for its heavy clusters of sweet, deep-purple fruit that evaluations have repeatedly found especially rich in anthocyanins and overall polyphenol content compared with other named saskatoon cultivars. It forms an upright, multi-stemmed, moderately suckering clump that produces fewer new suckers per plant than many other saskatoon selections, making it a bit tidier to manage in a mixed hedgerow or orchard row. Plant in full sun and well-drained soil; fruit holds up well in storage, making Nelson a good choice where berries will be picked over several days rather than all at once. Prune out the oldest canes periodically to keep the clump productive and encourage new fruiting wood.

planting.note: Plant dormant suckers or container stock in early spring into well-drained, cold-prairie-adapted soil, giving the clump room to widen as it establishes.

directions: Lee #3 is a saskatoon selection bred by Lloyd Lee of Barrhead, Alberta from a cross of the 'Northline' and 'Pembina' cultivars, combining traits of two long-standing prairie favorites. It produces good-flavored, juicy fruit suited to both fresh eating and preserving, carried on an upright, cold-hardy, multi-stemmed shrub typical of the species. Give it full sun and well-drained soil, and expect some root suckering over time as the clump matures and widens. Because saskatoons are only partially self-fruitful, planting Lee #3 alongside a second saskatoon cultivar will improve pollination and yield.
sources: Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada saskatoon cultivar trials

common_name: R.J. Hilton Allegheny Serviceberry (Compact Vase-Shaped Selection)

planting.note: Plant a container or balled-and-burlapped specimen in fall or spring into moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil, siting it where its narrow vase shape can be appreciated as a specimen tree.

directions: R.J. Hilton is a compact, narrow, vase-shaped selection of Allegheny serviceberry, noticeably smaller and tidier in habit than typical seedling-grown A. laevis. Large pink flower buds open to white star-shaped blossoms in April, emerging alongside bronze-red new foliage that matures to dark green and then turns yellow-orange to red in fall. It tolerates wind and urban pollution reasonably well, making it a workable choice for smaller gardens, courtyards, and even large containers or roof gardens where a full-size shadbush would be too large. Site it in full sun to light shade in humus-rich, evenly moist, slightly acidic soil for the best flowering, fruiting, and fall color.
sources: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: John Blue Darrow's Blueberry (Dwarf Evergreen Native Blueberry)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into acidic, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants close together if a dense groundcover-like mass is desired.

directions: John Blue is a dwarf, mounding selection of Darrow's blueberry, a low-growing evergreen Vaccinium native to sandy pinelands and scrub of the Southeast. Small, blue-green leaves stay on the plant through winter, giving the low mounds year-round structure in a border or rock garden, while tiny pink-white spring flowers give way to small, sweet, powder-blue summer berries. It is far more drought-tolerant than highbush or rabbiteye blueberries once established, reflecting its native habit on deep, dry, sandy soils, but still needs consistently acidic soil to thrive. Use it as a low edging or small-scale groundcover in full sun, and avoid heavy fertilization or alkaline amendments that highbush blueberry culture would otherwise call for.
sources: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
North Carolina Botanical Garden native plant records

common_name: Native Blue Southern Ornamental Blueberry (Compact Evergreen Groundcover)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, mass-planting for a low evergreen groundcover effect.

directions: Native Blue is a low, spreading, evergreen selection of Darrow's blueberry grown chiefly for ornamental groundcover use in Gulf South and Southeastern landscapes rather than for fruit production. Fine-textured, silvery-blue evergreen foliage forms a dense, tidy mat that stays attractive through winter, while light pink spring flowers are followed by a light crop of small, sweet, powdery-blue berries that wildlife readily take. Because it derives from a scrub and sandhill native, it performs well in lean, fast-draining, acidic sandy soils and tolerates considerably more drought than typical highbush or rabbiteye blueberry cultivars. Use it in mass plantings, as a border edge, or on slopes where a low native evergreen groundcover with some wildlife food value is wanted.
sources: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
University of Florida IFAS Extension native plant records
